framework: FBISE Assessment Framework (National Curriculum of Pakistan 2022-23)
subject: Physics

source.publisher: Federal Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education
source.licence: Government publication; structure + our own wording only

outcomes.text: Make sensible estimates of physical quantities met in this course.
Write derived units as products or quotients of SI base units.
Check whether a physical equation is homogeneous using dimensions.
Derive simple formulae using dimensional analysis.
Judge the accuracy and precision of data from measuring instruments.
Find the uncertainty of a derived quantity by adding absolute, fractional or percentage uncertainties.
Explain why every measurement carries some uncertainty.
Split a 2-D vector into two perpendicular components.
Describe dot and cross products of vectors and their properties.
Derive the equations of motion for uniform acceleration from definitions and graphs.
Solve straight-line and 2-D problems with the equations of motion, including free fall.
Analyse projectile motion without air resistance: height, range, time of flight and best launch angle.
Predict qualitatively how air resistance changes a projectile's path.
Express angles in radians.
Define and calculate angular displacement, velocity and acceleration using s=rθ and v=rω.
Use the equations of angular motion to solve rotation problems.
Explain qualitatively motion on a curved path caused by a perpendicular force.
Define and calculate centripetal force using F=mω²r and F=mv²/r.
Analyse circular motion where tension, friction, gravity or a normal force supplies the centripetal force.
Explain why objects in orbiting satellites seem weightless.
Describe how artificial gravity counters weightlessness.
Explain how a centrifuge separates materials using centripetal force.
Use conservation of momentum on simple one- and two-dimensional collision problems.
Analyse elastic collisions using conserved kinetic energy and equal approach and separation speeds.
Justify why momentum is conserved in a closed system although kinetic energy may change.
Define and calculate moment of inertia and angular momentum.
Derive and use the relation between torque, moment of inertia and angular acceleration.
State and apply conservation of angular momentum, with real examples such as flywheels, gyroscopes and skaters.
Tell crystalline, glassy, amorphous and polymeric solids apart by structure.
Describe tensile and compressive deformation of solids by a force.
Define and use stress, strain and the Young modulus.
Describe an experiment to find the Young modulus of a metal wire.
Describe elastic and plastic deformation and the elastic limit.
Use the area under a force-extension graph as work done.
Find elastic potential energy from the graph and use E=½Fx=½kx².
Derive the kinetic energy formula from the equations of motion.
Find work done from a force-displacement graph.
Tell conservative from non-conservative forces.
Use the work-energy theorem in a resistive medium.
Justify and use Archimedes' principle of flotation.
Explain how ships are built to float.
Define steady, incompressible and non-viscous flow of an ideal fluid.
Use the equation of continuity to solve problems.
Explain why squeezing a rubber pipe's end speeds up the flow.
Justify continuity as conservation of mass.
Explain how different flow rates produce pressure differences (Bernoulli effect).
Explain and apply Bernoulli's equation for horizontal and vertical flow.
Analyse real uses of the Bernoulli effect such as atomisers, spinning balls and Venturi ducts.
Explain why real fluids are viscous.
Describe how viscous forces retard an object moving through a fluid.
Describe superfluidity as zero viscosity and its consequences.
State that regions at equal temperature are in thermal equilibrium.
Relate a rise in temperature to more internal energy.

subtopics.title: Ideal gas law and kinetic theory

outcomes.text: Apply the ideal gas equation pV=nRT and pV=NkT.
State that the Boltzmann constant is k=R/N_A.
Describe the assumptions of kinetic theory and when real gases act ideally.
Explain with particles how pressure, volume and temperature of a gas relate.
Use the equation and graph linking pressure and volume at constant temperature.
Use W=pΔV for work when gas volume changes at constant pressure.
Tell work done by a gas from work done on a gas.
Define and use the first law Q=ΔU+W.
Justify the first law as conservation of energy.
Relate a body's rise in temperature to its increased internal energy.

subtopics.title: Heat engines and the second law

outcomes.text: State the working principle of a heat engine.
Describe reversible and irreversible processes.
State and explain the second law of thermodynamics.
State the working principle of the Carnot engine.
Describe a refrigerator as a heat engine run in reverse.
State that the Carnot cycle limits efficiency to 1 - Tcold/Thot.
Explain that higher temperature raises the disorder of a system.
Explain that rising entropy means degraded energy.
Explain that energy is degraded in all natural processes.
Recognise that systems become less orderly over time.
Explain entropy as a measure of particle disorder.
Use intensity = power/area and intensity proportional to amplitude squared.
Explain why a moving source changes the frequency heard by a still observer.
Use the observed-frequency formula for a moving source.
Explain uses of the Doppler effect in radar, sonar, astronomy and medicine.
Explain that polarization happens only with transverse waves.
Define and use Malus's law I=I0cos²θ.
Explain how polaroids are used in sky photography and stress analysis.
Use the principle of superposition to solve problems.
Tell constructive from destructive interference.
Explain how noise-cancelling headphones use superposition.
Explain coherence.
Illustrate experiments showing stationary waves with microwaves, strings and air columns.
Explain how a stationary wave forms using graphs.
Explain how harmonics form in stationary waves.
Analyse diffraction experiments and how gap width compared with wavelength matters.
Explain beats as pulsing from two close frequencies.
Show how beats arise in musical instruments.
Describe gravitational waves qualitatively.
State that a passing gravitational wave periodically stretches and compresses a body.
State that gravitational waves pass through Earth with very tiny amplitude.
Describe how interferometers detect gravitational waves.

subtopics.title: Electric field strength and field lines

outcomes.text: State that an electric field is a field of force.
Define and calculate field strength using F=qE and E=ΔV/Δd.
Represent electric fields with field lines.
Describe how a uniform field moves charged particles.
State that outside a charged sphere, its charge acts like a point charge at the centre.
Explain how a Faraday cage shields its inside.
State and use Coulomb's law for two point charges.
Use E=kQ/r² for the field of a point charge.
Describe how ferrofluids respond to magnet poles and where they are used.
Use I=Anvq for current in a conductor.
State and use V=W/Q.
State and use P=IV, P=I²R and P=V²/R.
State and use R=ρL/A.
State that an LDR's resistance falls as light gets brighter.
Define and use electromotive force.
Tell e.m.f. from potential difference using energy ideas.
Explain how internal resistance affects terminal voltage.
Explain internal resistance and its effects on external circuits.
State Kirchhoff's first law as conservation of charge.
State Kirchhoff's second law as conservation of energy.
Derive the combined resistance of resistors in series.
Derive and use the combined resistance of resistors in parallel.
Use Kirchhoff's laws to solve simple circuits.
State and use the potentiometer principle to compare potential differences.
Explain the galvanometer in null methods.
Explain thermistors and LDRs in potential dividers.
Explain how carbon fibres let inspectors check a concrete bridge by conduction.

subtopics.title: Magnetic fields and forces on currents

outcomes.text: Define and explain magnetic fields.
State that a current-carrying conductor can feel a force in a magnetic field.
Use F=BIL sinθ with Fleming's left-hand rule.
Define magnetic flux density.
Use F=Bqv sinθ to solve problems.
Describe a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field.
Explain velocity selection using electric and magnetic fields.
Sketch field patterns of a straight wire, flat coil and solenoid.
State that an iron core strengthens a solenoid's field.
Explain the forces between current-carrying conductors and find their direction.
Define magnetic flux.
Use Φ=BA to solve problems.
Use magnetic flux linkage.
Explain experiments showing Faraday's and Lenz's laws.
Use Faraday's and Lenz's laws to solve problems.
Explain how seismometers detect earthquakes using induction.
Tell inertial from non-inertial frames of reference.
Describe why Einstein's constant speed of light matters.
Describe how a constant c makes space and time relative.
State the postulates of special relativity.
Explain simultaneity, mass-energy equivalence, length contraction, time dilation and mass increase.
State that space-time treats time as a fourth dimension.
State that nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear processes.
Describe the composition, mass and charge of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
Explain that an antiparticle has equal mass and opposite charge.
State which neutrinos are produced in beta-minus and beta-plus decay.
Explain why alpha energies are discrete but beta energies are continuous.
Describe quarks, antiquarks and the six flavours.
Describe protons and neutrons by their quark makeup.
State that hadrons are baryons or mesons.
Describe quark changes in beta-minus and beta-plus decay.
Describe protons and neutrons by their quark composition.
State that a hadron is a baryon of three quarks or a meson of a quark and antiquark.
State that electrons and neutrinos are leptons.
State W, Z, gluon and photon as exchange particles.
State that the Higgs boson is linked to particle mass.
Explain that every subatomic particle has an antiparticle.
Explain that several theories exist about where mass and force come from.
Explain how particle accelerators work and what they are used for.
Explain antimatter as the counterpart of matter.
Illustrate that antiparticles have the same mass but opposite charge.
State that most observable matter is ordinary matter.
Describe the matter-antimatter asymmetry as an unsolved mystery.
Describe annihilation reactions.
Check equipment works safely before an experiment.
Keep the workspace uncrowded and safe.
Keep a safe distance from other workers.
Suggest what harm physical, chemical, biological or safety hazards could cause.
State that asking the lab instructor is better than guessing with new apparatus.
Set up apparatus correctly without help.
Follow written instructions and diagrams, including circuit diagrams.
Collect an appropriate quantity of data.
Repeat readings where suitable.
Take measurements over the widest possible range.
Estimate the absolute uncertainty in measurements.
Express uncertainty as absolute or percentage and convert between them.
Take absolute uncertainty of repeated readings as half their range.
Use a false origin when plotting graphs.
Draw lines or curves of best fit.
Draw tangents and find gradients.
Relate straight-line graphs to y=mx+c and derive gradient and intercept expressions.
Read coordinates from a trend line.
Read values from a graph's trend line.
Find the y-intercept of a line or tangent, including with a false origin.
Draw conclusions from experiments, including finding constants.
Explain whether data supports a hypothesis and make predictions.
Decide whether data supports a relationship containing a constant.
Compare percentage difference of constants with a given uncertainty and conclude.
Identify limitations in an experimental procedure.
Identify the biggest sources of uncertainty.
Suggest an arrangement that improves accuracy or extends the investigation.
Describe such changes clearly in words or diagrams.
